meta.title: Analysis of Space Research through Neural Topic Modeling leveraging Large Language Models
meta.authorsHtml: Ruben Belo<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Marta Guimarães<sup>1, 2</sup>, Cláudia Soares<sup>1</sup>

abstract: The rapid growth of space-related research, spanning disciplines from Earth observation to robotics and machine learning, presents challenges for efficiently navigating and contextualizing the literature. Traditional categorization approaches struggle to capture emerging themes and crossdisciplinary connections. In this work, we present a data-driven analysis of space science publications from the wellknown preprint server arXiv, using neural topic modeling enhanced with large language models to uncover latent topics and track their evolution over time. Our methodology identifies major research themes, highlights the emergence of multimodal and self-supervised approaches, and captures methodological trends within high-prevalence topics. This analysis provides a resource for researchers and newcomers alike to navigate the rapidly expanding literature, supporting informed exploration and fostering interdisciplinary understanding.

blocks.html: Scientific publications are growing in number, posing challenges for researchers to stay current. This is particularly true in space science (Fig. 1), which spans multiple disciplines (e.g., Earth Observation and Space Debris Mitigation to robotics and machine learning) [1–10]. Space-related publications on arXiv have increased dramatically since the mid-2000s, with Computer Science emerging as a major contributor by 2025. This reflects the growing influence of data-driven and computational methods in space research, reshaping how the field is organized and understood.

The growing volume and cross-disciplinary nature of space research increases the risk of overlooking key findings and hinders collaboration across disciplines [11–13]. Recent work, including Pathfinder, a semantic LLM-based framework for literature exploration [12], and LLM-driven knowledge discovery for lunar dust research addressing tagging and retrieval limitations [13], attempts to tackle this challenge.

In this study, we collect space-related papers from arXiv spanning 1996 to 2025 to create a dataset of space research publications. We analyze it using Neural Topic Model (NTM) and Large Language Models (LLMs), a data-driven approach that allows topics and themes to emerge directly from the documents rather than relying on predefined categories, such as arXiv’s subject tags, which impose a fixed structure on a dynamic field. The increasing contribution of Computer Science to space research further illustrates that these boundaries are constantly shifting, and strict taxonomies.

blocks.html: Our focus is to provide an analysis of the evolution of space research topics over time, highlighting emerging directions and thematic growth (e.g., exploring the relationship between the Space domain and Computer Science). We uncover influential methods, track the development of research themes, and identify links that fixed classification systems would obscure. Using this methodology, which combines NTM and LLM for temporal analysis, the results demonstrate that the recovered topics and trends align with what experts in the field would expect to see. This approach produces a structured map of space science research, offering insights that can support both established researchers and newcomers in navigating this rapidly expanding domain. Topic Modeling. Given a corpus D = {d1, . . . , dN} of N documents over a vocabulary of size V , topic modeling aims to identify K latent topics capturing the main semantic patterns. Each topic k is a probability distribution over the vocabulary, ϕk ∈∆V [15, 16], where ∆V is the probability simplex of dimension V .

For each document di, the model infers a topic representation θi ∈∆K, describing the proportion of each topic. Document words are assumed generated from these topic proportions combined with the topic-word distributions.

In neural topic modeling, this generative structure is parameterized with neural networks. Documents are typically represented as bag-of-words vectors and mapped to latent topic representations via an encoder network. A decoder then reconstructs the document’s word distribution using the learned topic–word parameters. This formulation preserves interpretable topic–word and document–topic structures while enabling efficient learning through gradient-based optimization. Examples of this approach include Neural Variational Document Model (NVDM) [17], WeTe [18], and ETM [19].
Other types of topic models, include probabilistic models such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [20], cluster-based models like BERTopic [21], and a representative LLM-based model, TopicGPT [22].

NTM with LLM-ITL. LLM-in-the-loop (LLM-ITL) [15] integrates an LLM into the training loop of a NTM to enhance topic interpretability without reducing efficiency. At each step, the top words of a topic ϕk are passed to the LLM, which proposes semantically improved replacements. These are incorporated via an Optimal Transport [15, 23, 24] alignment objective minimizing the discrepancy between the topic-word distributions and the refined targets.

Hallucinations are mitigated using a confidenceweighted mechanism, and a warm-up phase ensures the NTM first learns corpus-relevant representations. The LLM also assigns descriptive labels to topics, producing humanreadable summaries of each latent theme.

To study the temporal evolution of space-related research, we constructed a longitudinal corpus of publications from arXiv [14], spanning 1996-2025 (Fig. 1). We focused on core areas of space systems research, including: (i) Space Operations; (ii) Space Debris and Space Traffic Management; (iii) Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC); (iv) Earth Observation and Remote Sensing; (v) Mission Planning and Onboard Autonomy.
Queries were combined with relevant arXiv subject categories across Physics, Astronomy, Mathematics, and Computer Science to ensure interdisciplinary coverage.

Each document includes title, abstract, publication date, and subject categories, with duplicates removed via arXiv identifiers. Organizing the dataset temporally enables yearby-year (or finer) analyses.

blocks.html: Our methodology. This analysis comprises two components: (1) characterizing the temporal evolution of research topics and (2) tracking technique development within those topics.

As a preparatory step, we evaluated four topic modeling approaches: LDA [20], BERTopic [21], Embedding Clustering Regularized Topic Model (ECRTM) [25], and NVDM [17]. Additionally, we applied the LLM-ITL enhancement [15] to both ECRTM and NVDM. Given the un-supervised nature of the task, model comparison was based on both quantitative metrics and label interpretability. Quantitatively, we evaluated topic quality using Topic Quality (TQ) [18], which combines topic coherence (TC) [26] and topic diversity (TD) [19] with TQ = TC × TD, thereby capturing both the semantic consistency and distinctiveness of topic words.

blocks.caption: How topics evolve over time (yearly counts). From the initial K = 25 topics, we select the top 12 based on total document count over the last three years. Each topic’s area is divided into three stacked layers corresponding to documents where the topic ranked 1st, 2nd, and 3rd in the inferred topic-proportion vector θi from bottom to top respectively.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The resulting TQ scores for different numbers of topics are reported in Table 1. In addition to these quantitative measures, we assessed the interpretability of the generated topic labels. This evaluation showed that NVDM enhanced with LLM-ITL produced the most suitable topic labels for this study. Integrating an LLM enables refinement of topic labels across epochs and improves the coherence of the top words associated with each topic.

Temporal Dynamics. We fit the selected model with K = 25 latent topics to the constructed corpus. To analyze temporal dynamics, we aggregate document–topic assignments at the yearly level and, for each topic k, track the count of documents for which it ranks 1st, 2nd, or 3rd in the inferred topic-proportion vector θi. Topics are then ranked by total document count over the last three years, and the top 12 are selected for visualization. Fig. 2 illustrates the resulting prevalence trajectories.

Intra-Topic Technique Evolution. To track shifts in research focus within a topic, we divide the documents that rank 1st and 2nd in θi into temporal epochs and cluster abstracts using DBSCAN [27] on sentence embeddings. Hyperparameters are tuned to favor many small, cohesive clusters, highlighting fine-grained methodological sub-themes. Each cluster is summarized with an LLM through iterative prompting until convergence or five iterations [28]. The most representative summaries are then manually curated to produce the trace of methodological evolution.

Topic Dynamics Over Time. Fig. 2 shows a clear stratification among the 12 most prevalent topics. Multimodal Reasoning grows most rapidly, with near-exponential acceleration after 2020. Image Processing, Autonomous Mobility, and Weather Forecast follow similar but slower trajectories, remaining consistently primary topics.

Dimensionality Reduction, Motion Planning, and Signal Distortion grows steadily but moderately. Dimensionality Reduction and Signal Distortion mostly appear as secondary themes since the majority of document counts derive from 2nd and 3rd rank assignments in θi. Motion Planning is primarily first-ranked, comparable to Multimodal Reasoning. Image Classification displays an early plateau: despite a substantial document base prior to 2020 (likely reflecting its centrality during the early deep learning era) its growth has since stagnated, with a possible decline suggesting a migration of research interest toward multimodal and self-supervised learning as the field matures. Other topics remain marginal, forming the peripheral tail.

blocks.title: How a Topic Evolves Over the Years?

blocks.html: We analyze the evolution of two topics over time: Multimodal Reasoning Fig. 3, Weather Forecast Fig. 4 and Space Travel Fig 5.

blocks.caption: Evolution of Multimodal Reasoning. The curve shows documents per year, with shaded regions indicating temporal epochs. Boxes summarize dominant techniques and sub-themes identified using clustering and LLM-based summarization.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: Reinforcement Learning (RL). Appeared in Sim-to- Real robot navigation and collision avoidance (1996–2020), reflecting interest in autonomous systems. By 2023, RL research expanded to multi-agent collision avoidance, including spacecraft and swarm systems. In 2025, RL became part of LLM-driven robotics, integrating with diffusion-based planning and motion control to support navigation, manipulation, and spacecraft autonomy in both single- and multi-agent settings. Generative Models. Began with generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders (1996–2020) for synthetic data generation and domain adaptation, addressing the scarcity of labeled satellite imagery. From 2021, these models supported synthetic geospatial imagery and reconstruction. By 2023, diffusion models emerged, complementing existing approaches for satellite image synthesis, super-resolution, and 3D reconstruction. In 2024–2025, diffusion models further advanced cross-view synthesis, geospatial data augmentation, reconstruction, and crosssensor translation, enabling multimodal Earth observation across optical and synthetic aperture radar.

blocks.caption: Evolution of Weather Forecast. The curve shows documents per year, with shaded regions indicating temporal epochs. Boxes summarize dominant techniques and sub-themes identified using clustering and LLM-based summarization.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: Progressive Integration of Language and Vision. Began around 2022 with early vision-language interactions, including language-guided visual grounding and visual question answering for satellite imagery. By 2023, foundation models enabled large-scale pretrained architectures that supported multimodal tasks such as image captioning, retrieval, and visual question answering, while self-supervised pretraining improved representation learning across multi-sensor datasets. In 2024 and 2025, research focused on adapting these pretrained models to geospatial tasks, enabling prompt-based interaction, scene interpretation, change detection, and multimodal reasoning, consolidating vision and language integration for scalable Earth observation and geospatial intelligence.

Shift from Label-Dependent to Self-Supervised and Multimodal Learning. Early deep learning relied heavily on labeled datasets for classification and segmentation, which limited scalability across Earth observation tasks. From around 2021, self-supervised and multimodal methods emerged to handle sparse labels and integrate multiple sensor modalities. Domain adaptation and semi-supervised strategies complemented these approaches, enabling models to transfer knowledge across datasets and reduce dependence on annotated data. By 2023–2025, these techniques, often combined with pretrained models, supported scalable representation learning.

Overview. The Weather Forecast topic is relatively homogeneous: core themes—satellite/remote sensing, environmental monitoring, spatiotemporal forecasting, and socio-economic mapping—remain consistent. The main evolution lies in methodology rather than research focus.

Machine Learning for Earth Observation. Early work applied ML and deep learning to satellite and aerial imagery for environmental monitoring, land cover mapping, weather and ocean prediction, atmospheric analysis, and disaster assessment, with multi-sensor remote sensing establishing the foundation for large-scale Earth observation.

Spatiotemporal Forecasting and Multi-Sensor Fusion. Recent trends integrate temporal and multi-sensor data for forecasting climate, space weather, and environmental hazards. Techniques include CNNs, LSTMs, U-Nets, attention mechanisms, and transformers, supporting applications in wildfire/deforestation risk, precision agriculture, and atmospheric monitoring.

Autonomous Monitoring and Disaster Assessment. From 2021, ML enabled rapid, autonomous analysis of imagery for disasters, infrastructure, vegetation, and socioeconomic indicators, with multi-sensor fusion improving scalable monitoring of crops, land use, and environmental hazards.

blocks.html: Multimodal and Foundation Models. From 2023 onward, multimodal fusion and foundation models supported high-resolution mapping, prediction, and integration of satellite and auxiliary data for disaster response, precision agriculture, and climate resilience.

Space Debris and NEO Management. Early work addressed space object tracking, orbital dynamics, and collision analysis. From 2011 onwards, techniques expanded to asteroid and near-Earth object (NEO) deflection, mitigation strategies, and trajectory modeling. By 2023–2025, AI and machine learning were incorporated for autonomous debris tracking, collision avoidance, risk prediction, and active mitigation, supporting LEO sustainability and planetary defense. Propulsion, Navigation, and Mission Optimization. Initial advances focused on fusion, electrostatic, and beamed-energy propulsion for orbit raising and deep-space travel. Later trends included optimization frameworks for low-thrust trajectories, multi-body orbital dynamics, and trajectory planning. Recent work (2024–2025) integrates AI/ML methods for trajectory and attitude optimization, autonomous navigation, and in-space mission planning, including servicing, collision avoidance, and resource allocation. Astrometry, Observatories, and Space-Based Sensing. From 1996–2015, research explored astrometric missions (e.g., Gaia, ASTROD, Euclid), space-based interferometry, and celestial object characterization. Later, studies included small satellite constellations for Earth observation, lunar and asteroid missions, and formation flying for space telescopes. By 2025, advanced sensing, AI-driven perception, and small spacecraft networks support deep-space exploration, photonics experiments, and planetary science investigations. AI, Autonomy, and Robotics in Space Operations. While early spacecraft control relied on classical optimization, from 2018 AI methods began supporting guidance, orbit prediction, and resource management. By 2022–2023, machine learning and reinforcement learning enabled autonomous spacecraft navigation, perception, and control. Recent developments (2024–2025) focus on AI-driven autonomous robotics for debris mitigation, on-orbit servicing, and mission planning, as well as 3D reconstruction, digital twins, and multimodal autonomy.

The growth of Multimodal Reasoning reflects the expanding role of machine learning in specialized domains. In contrast, the plateau observed in Image Classification suggests a maturing field, as researchers increasingly explore alternative directions. The analyzed topics indicate that our approach produces interpretable themes that align with domain expert expectations, supporting its usefulness as a tool for literature analysis.

Regarding limitations, we use K = 25 topics as it provides a human-interpretable level of granularity, although finer decompositions could reveal additional structure. The use of LLMs for summarization and labeling, while effective, may introduce minor errors or overlook nuanced details within clusters. Additionally, because dataset construction relies on keyword-based retrieval, some documents may only be tangentially related to space research.

Future work includes a broader analysis that maps individual articles to topics to enable a survey-like synthesis of the field, as well as applying this methodology to specific sub-areas of space research for more fine-grained insights.

This work analyzes publicly available scientific literature obtained from the arXiv repository using topic modeling and large language models to study the evolution of research topics. The study does not involve personal, sensitive, or proprietary data. No direct ethical risks are associated with the methods or data used in this work.

This research was carried out under Project “Artificial Intelligence Fights Space Debris” Nº C626449889-0046305 co-funded by Recovery and Resilience Plan and NextGeneration EU Funds (www.recuperarportugal.gov.pt), and by NOVA LINCS (UIDB/04516/2020) with the financial support of FCT.IP.

This work analyzes publicly available scientific publications from the arXiv repository to study the evolution of research topics in space science using neural topic models and large language models. The work does not involve personal, sensitive, or proprietary data. However, automated topic discovery and LLM-assisted topic labeling may introduce biases, hallucinated associations, or oversimplified interpretations of complex scientific contributions. Consequently, the results should be interpreted as exploratory analytical tools that complement rather than replace expert domain judgment, and should be used transparently and responsibly when informing literature surveys or research policy discussions.
